outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no proof or disproof that there are infinitely many base-b repunit primes, for any admissible base b, has appeared in any source I could reach; the only movement is new single instances in particular bases (a base-10 repunit proven prime on 26 May 2025, generalized repunit primes in bases 92365, 74968, 124750, 940, 58425, 21 and −3) and two 2024 papers on neighbouring questions.
problem_asks: (1) The domain: every integer b that is not a perfect power and is not of the form −4k⁴ for an integer k. The Wikipedia Repunit article, which the bullet's wording follows, states the conjecture for integers with |b| > 1; the perfect-power and −4k⁴ clauses exclude b = 0, ±1 and −4, −64, −324, and so on. (2) For each such b: are there infinitely many n for which Rₙ(b) = (bⁿ − 1)/(b − 1) is prime, i.e. infinitely many base-b repunit primes? The statement is one yes/no question per admissible b, written as a single question over all of them; settling it for one b does not settle it for another. It asks for infinitude only, not for density or for the count of such primes up to a bound.

events.delivers: One base-10 repunit prime, proven prime, with index 1031. Covers base 10 only and a single instance; it says nothing about whether there are infinitely many repunit primes in any base.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: no infinitude result for any base.

events.what_happened: Paul Bourdelais posted 'A Generalized Repunit Conjecture' to the NMBRTHRY mailing list, cited by OEIS and by Wikipedia's Repunit article (footnote 10). Per OEIS comments by Bourdelais it posits that prime-occurrence rates across bases eventually converge to a common relative rate, with conjectured constant G = 0.56145948. events.delivers: A conjecture about asymptotic rates of prime occurrence across bases, with a conjectured constant. It is a different question from whether base-b repunit primes are infinite for a given b: it compares bases in the limit, and it does not assert that any single base has infinitely many. Discounted as a neighbouring question.

events.doubts: The statement is known only through OEIS comments and the mailing-list link; the original posting was not read.
events.direction: A conjecture about rates across bases; it neither proves nor disproves infinitude for any base.

summary: No source I could reach proves or disproves that there are infinitely many base-b repunit primes for any admissible base, and no source claims to. The Wikipedia bullet (List of unsolved problems in mathematics, Number theory > Prime numbers) has no citation and links only to the Repunit article, which states the conjecture for integers with |b| > 1 and adds the perfect-power and −4k⁴ exclusions, with an Aurifeuillian reason for the latter. I searched for the name under several phrasings, for the Bourdelais 'Generalized Repunit Conjecture', for recent arXiv and journal work, and for AI involvement (38 searches in total). The movement since January 2024 is confined to single instances. (i) R109297, the base-10 repunit with index 109297, is proven prime by an ECPP certificate submitted on 26 May 2025 (Prime Pages submission record, FactorDB status P, Wikipedia), though Prime Pages still lists it PRP. (ii) Generalized repunit primes in bases 92365 (Feb 2024), 74968 (Jul 2024), 124750 (Sep 2024), 940 (Jan 2025, PRP) and 58425 (Sep 2025, PRP) appear on the Prime Pages top-20 list. (iii) OEIS A007658 (prime repunits in base −3) gained a(28) = 2674381 on 22 Mar 2024 and a(29) = 7034611 on 4 Dec 2024. (iv) OEIS A127996 (base 21) gained a(8) = 3078871 on 1 Jun 2026, credited to Bourdelais, with no proven/probable status stated. Each adds one exponent to one base's list, which is a finite instance of a question asking for infinitely many, so I record them as events and do not treat them as moving the infinitude question. Two other in-window papers are neighbouring questions: Santos and Costa (Intermaths 2024) prove that no repunit value is a perfect power, which concerns values rather than primality and not the base clause; and Grantham (arXiv:2410.03677, Integers 2024) bounds Goormaghtigh primes below 10⁷⁰⁰, which concerns repunits in two bases. Pre-window events are recorded for completeness: the base-10 milestones (R1031 in 1986, R49081 and R86453 probable primes and proofs, R5794777 and R8177207 probable primes in 2021, R109297 probable prime in 2007), the Dubner 1993 table for bases up to 99, and Bourdelais's 2009 conjecture about convergence of prime-occurrence rates across bases with constant G = 0.56145948, which is a different question. Close calls: (a) whether R109297 counts as proven, given the status conflict; (b) whether a single new base-b prime should count as moving a 'quantity named in the statement' (the count of base-b repunit primes) or as one more instance of an existential claim; I have treated it as the second, consistent with the Collatz example in the brief; (c) whether the base-21 a(8) and the top-20 base entries are proven or probable, which the sources do not say. AI involvement: no AI system is named in any source touching this problem. The AI search covered OpenAI's Astra announcement (1 Aug 2026; the primary page returned 403, so only secondary coverage was read), Anthropic's Riemann post (10 Aug 2026; opened, and it mentions no repunit or base-b prime result), Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve paper (arXiv 2511.02864; read in three chunks by a summarising fetch, which names AlphaEvolve, Deep Think, AlphaProof and Gemini 2.5 and lists no repunit problem), and AI results on Erdős problems. None bears on this problem. The base-b repunit questions also get no AI attribution from the OEIS or Prime Pages entries, which credit human users and proof-code handles.
competing_reading: One could treat each new base-b prime as moving the quantity the statement names, since the number of base-b repunit primes is exactly what is asked about. On that reading the 2024–2026 instances (and the 2026 base-21 term) are growth in the count, and a series of such additions would be evidence for the conjecture. The stronger reading is the one I used: the statement asks whether that count is unbounded, and a finite count that grows by one still says nothing about unboundedness, as with the Collatz verification example in the brief. A second reading says the R109297 proof is a proven instance that should count as a restricted resolution of a part of the problem in base 10; I do not think the statement asks for any particular base, so that reading does not apply.
what_would_settle_it: For infinitude: a proof (or a published heuristic-free argument) that Rₙ(b) is prime for infinitely many n for some admissible b, or conversely a proof of finiteness for some b, which I found no sign of. For the record: the Prime Pages status of R109297 and the FactorDB certificate checked with an independent verifier such as Primo; the proven/probable status of the base-21 a(8) and the 2024–2025 top-20 entries; the full text of Santos and Costa (base of R_n, and the acknowledgements) and of the 1993 Dubner table; and a full arXiv search of 2024–2026 for 'repunit' and 'generalized repunit', which I could only approximate through the web search index.

judgement.why: The statement asks, for each admissible base b, whether infinitely many base-b repunits are prime. Every prime or probable-prime discovery and proof in the record is one more finite instance in one base, so each is scored instances (F5), including the 2025 R109297 ECPP proof. The proof's Prime Pages status conflict does not matter for scope. A single new prime is not a case: no base's infinitude question is settled by it. I scored Bourdelais's 2009 rate-convergence conjecture none, because it is a heuristic conjecture and settles nothing. Santos–Costa (repunit values are not perfect powers) and Grantham (Goormaghtigh primes) answer different questions, so both are variant. No AI system appears in any event.
judgement.doubts: Searches of arXiv for 2024–2026 were approximated through a web index, and several OEIS base-b sequences were not opened. Neither gap could change the result, since any further hit would also be a finite instance unless it were an infinitude proof.
